objectives: Explain why multiple heads beat one big head

slides.title: Part 1 — One head is not enough
slides.body: Single-head attention computes one weighted average per token — every token's output the same way. But a model needs to track syntax (local attention) *and* resolve coreference (long-range) *and* copy patterns, all at once. Multi-head attention is how one layer does many things.

slides.title: Run attention h times in parallel
slides.body:
**Multi-head attention** runs $h$ independent attention computations side by side. Each head has its *own* learned $W_Q^h, W_K^h, W_V^h$, so each can specialize: one head learns locality, another pronoun resolution, another induction (copy the token that followed a previous occurrence).

The heatmap shows one head's pattern; in a real layer there are $h$ of these, each different. Outputs are concatenated and projected back to $d_{model}$.

slides.title: The shapes (and why it's the same parameter count)
slides.body:
Each head projects $d_{model}$ down to $d_k = d_{model}/h$. With $d_{model}=512, h=8$, each head works in 64 dims.

```
X: [batch, seq, d_model]
  → per-head W_Q^h, W_K^h, W_V^h
Q_h,K_h,V_h: [batch, seq, d_k]
  → scaled dot-product attention
head_h: [batch, seq, d_k]
  → concat over h heads → [batch, seq, d_model]
  → output projection W_O
out: [batch, seq, d_model]
```

Key realization: total parameters ≈ one big $d_{model}\times d_{model}$ attention. **Multi-head adds *diversity*, not capacity** — the same budget, spent on $h$ different patterns instead of one. $W_O$ is essential: it *mixes* the heads' outputs rather than leaving them side by side.

question.question: You set h=1 with the same total d_model. Versus an h=8 model, what changes?
options: Nothing — multi-head is just a parallelism optimization
The layer can learn only ONE attention pattern; h=8 could learn up to 8 different patterns at the same capacity
question.explanation: Same parameter count either way. The value of multi-head is representational diversity: h=8 can simultaneously be a locality head, an induction head, a punctuation head, etc. Collapsing to h=1 forces one pattern and reliably hurts language modeling.

slides.title: A catalog of head specializations
slides.body:
From BERT/GPT-2 interpretability work:

- **Previous-token heads** — attend one position back (copy what was just said).
- **Locality heads** — soft attention to a nearby window (syntax).
- **Punctuation heads** — fixate on commas/periods (phrase boundaries).
- **Coreference heads** — pronoun → antecedent.
- **Induction heads** (Olsson et al., 2022) — a two-layer circuit: a previous-token head in layer L feeds an induction head in L+1 that finds the earlier match and reads the token *after* it. This is the core of in-context pattern completion `A B … A → B`.

Not every head is clean: many are diffuse. The **superposition** hypothesis says heads pack multiple weak features together — which is why modern interpretability moved to sparse autoencoders.

question.question: An 'induction head' is best described as:
options: A single head that memorizes training sequences
A two-layer circuit (previous-token head → induction head) that completes patterns like 'A B … A → B' — the backbone of in-context learning
The first attention head in layer 0
A head that only attends to punctuation
question.explanation: Induction is compositional: a previous-token head writes 'the token before me' into the residual stream; a later induction head uses that to find the prior occurrence of the current token and attend to whatever followed it. This circuit is strongly linked to in-context learning ability.

slides.title: Part 3 — Grouped-query attention (the modern tweak)
slides.body: The one multi-head variant you'll see in nearly every recent model card.

slides.title: Share K and V to shrink the KV-cache
slides.body:
At inference, autoregressive generation caches every token's K and V for the whole context — with $h=32$ heads that's a lot of memory bandwidth.

**Grouped-query attention (GQA):** keep $h$ query heads but only $g$ shared KV groups (e.g. 32 query heads, 8 KV groups → each KV shared by 4). Memory drops ~4×, quality essentially preserved. **Multi-query attention (MQA)** is the extreme ($g=1$). LLaMA-2 70B and Mistral 7B use GQA with 8 KV heads. Training FLOPs barely change — the win is the inference KV-cache.

question.question: Why does GQA cut inference memory but leave training cost ≈ unchanged?
options: It only applies at inference; training uses full MHA
It shrinks the KV-cache (built only during autoregressive decoding); forward/backward FLOPs are dominated by matmuls that barely change
question.explanation: GQA's saving is the per-token K/V tensors cached across the context during generation — fewer KV groups ⇒ proportionally smaller cache. Training is FLOP-bound (full sequences, parallel), and those FLOPs are nearly the same, so train cost is ≈ unchanged.

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body:
- Multi-head = $h$ parallel attentions, each in a $d_{model}/h$ subspace, concatenated then mixed by $W_O$.
- It buys **diversity, not capacity** (same parameter count as one big attention).
- Heads specialize (previous-token, locality, induction…); some are in **superposition**.
- **GQA/MQA** share K/V to shrink the inference KV-cache at ~no quality cost.

**Next:** the [feed-forward network](/wiki/feed-forward-networks) — the per-token nonlinearity that holds most of the model's parameters — then [residuals](/wiki/residual-connections), [layer norm](/wiki/layer-normalization), and the full [transformer block](/wiki/transformer-block).
